- **Full snapshots every time**:  
  - Pros: trivial to reason about; each snapshot stands alone; restores are just “pick date → copy it back”; less chance of a subtle bug in backup logic breaking a whole chain.  
  - Cons: uses more disk and time, especially if the data grows large.

  - Pros: more space-efficient; large historical retention possible on the same disk.  
  - Cons: restores require applying a base plus one or more increments; if any piece in the chain is corrupt/missing, that snapshot may be unusable.

  - Every snapshot directory *looks* like a full backup, but unchanged files are hard links to the previous snapshot, so disk usage is closer to “incremental”; restores are just as easy as with full snapshots.
  - This is often the sweet spot for homelabs if you want efficiency without complex restore logic.

- Keep the “one directory per snapshot” model for all three services; it’s simple and makes restore procedures very straightforward.
- If your backup HDD has plenty of space and snapshot runs are fast enough, doing full snapshots every time is perfectly fine and arguably safer from an operational standpoint.
- If you start to worry about space or backup time, switch to the `--link-dest` pattern for memories/vikunja/n8n so you still get easy, self-contained snapshots but use disk more efficiently.
- Whichever you pick, add/prune policies (e.g., keep 7–14 daily, 4 weekly, 6–12 monthly) and practice at least one test restore so you know the exact commands and that your backups are actually usable.
